questions.q: Name the four Rashidun caliphs in chronological order and state the distinct method by which each assumed office.
questions.a: Abu Bakr (632–634): chosen by shura (consultation) of prominent companions at Saqifah. Umar (634–644): appointed by Abu Bakr's written testament (nass). Uthman (644–656): selected by a six-man electoral committee (shura) appointed by Umar. Ali (656–661): received bay'ah (oath of allegiance) from Medina companions after Uthman's assassination. A wrong answer (e.g., listing them as hereditary or all elected identically) reveals the student misses the evolving, ad-hoc nature of early caliphal legitimacy—a core board exam concept.

questions.q: Explain why the assassination of Uthman (656 CE) is considered the turning point that transformed a political dispute into a theological schism.
questions.a: Uthman's murder by rebels from Egypt and Iraq shattered the precedent that a caliph's life was inviolable once bay'ah was given. It forced the community to choose between: (a) punishing the rebels immediately (Ali's initial stance), (b) demanding justice for Uthman before allegiance (Muawiya's stance), or (c) rejecting both as illegitimate (Kharijite stance). This triple split embedded the question "Who has the right to judge a caliph?" into Islamic political theology. A wrong answer focusing only on "family rivalry" misses the constitutional crisis: the absence of a removal mechanism for a caliph.

questions.q: A historian argues: "The Rashidun caliphate was a continuation of pre-Islamic Arab tribal leadership (shaykh system) with Islamic vocabulary." Using evidence from the selection of Abu Bakr and Umar, evaluate this claim.
questions.a: Partial truth. Similarities: Abu Bakr's selection at Saqifah involved tribal leaders (Ansar vs. Muhajirun) negotiating like a tribal majlis; Umar's authority rested on personal charisma and military loyalty akin to a shaykh. Differences: The bay'ah was framed as a religious covenant (Quran 48:10), not just tribal loyalty; the caliph claimed authority over all Muslims, transcending tribe; Umar introduced the diwan (state registry) paying stipends by Islamic precedence (sabiqa), not tribal rank. A student who only sees continuity misses the revolutionary redefinition of political community from tribe to ummah.

questions.q: Compare the administrative innovations of Umar ibn al-Khattab (diwan, garrison cities, judicial qadis) with the Mauryan administration (as studied in Class 6). Identify two structural similarities and two fundamental differences in their theory of sovereignty.
questions.a: Similarities: Both created centralized revenue systems (diwan vs. samaharta) and appointed provincial governors with military-civil powers (amirs vs. kumaras). Both used written records for accountability. Differences: Mauryan sovereignty derived from the king as dharma-upholder (Ashoka's edicts); Rashidun sovereignty derived from the caliph as deputy (khalifat rasul Allah) implementing divine law (sharia). Mauryan officials were salaried bureaucrats; Rashidun stipends were hereditary rights based on Islamic precedence. A wrong answer conflating "bureaucracy" misses the theological source of legitimacy.

questions.q: "Ali's acceptance of arbitration at Siffin (657 CE) was a political necessity, not a theological compromise." Critique this statement using the Kharijite secession as evidence.
questions.a: The statement is defensible but incomplete. Politically, Ali faced mutiny in his own army (Qurra') who demanded arbitration to avoid fighting fellow Muslims. Theologically, he agreed to "arbitration by Quran" (not men), expecting the arbitrators to apply divine law. The Kharijites seceded precisely because they viewed any human arbitration over divine sovereignty (hakimiyya) as kufr—their slogan "La hukma illa lillah" (No judgment but God's) shows they saw it as theological betrayal. A student calling it purely political ignores that the Kharijite revolt created the first Islamic sect defined by a theological position on governance.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (632–661 CE) with six events that shows how the question of succession evolved from a practical problem into a doctrinal divide. Annotate each event with the competing legitimacy claim it generated.
questions.a: 1. 632 Saqifah: Abu Bakr elected → Legitimacy = Community consensus (ijma'). 2. 634 Umar's testament → Legitimacy = Predecessor's designation (nass). 3. 644 Electoral committee → Legitimacy = Restricted elite consultation (shura). 4. 656 Uthman murdered → Legitimacy crisis: Can a caliph be deposed/killed? 5. 656 Ali's bay'ah → Legitimacy = Broad bay'ah but contested by Muawiya (justice for Uthman). 6. 657 Siffin arbitration → Legitimacy = Divine judgment vs. human arbitration (Kharijite split). A poor timeline lists battles without the legitimacy claims, missing the intellectual history board exams test.
